reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / thyroid society guidance
clinicalPearls: Amiodarone is iodine-rich and lipophilic with a long half-life, so thyrotoxicosis can arise during treatment or months after the drug is stopped
Distinguishing type-1 from type-2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis is central because it determines whether antithyroid-drug or glucocorticoid therapy is used
Type 1 is iodine-induced excess hormone synthesis in an abnormal gland (nodular goitre or latent Graves) and is treated with antithyroid drugs
Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis releasing preformed hormone from a normal gland and responds to glucocorticoids
Mixed forms occur, and when the type is uncertain combined therapy is often used
Colour-flow Doppler helps discriminate the types, showing increased vascularity in type 1 and reduced or absent flow in type 2
New or worsening tachyarrhythmia or unexplained clinical deterioration in an amiodarone-treated patient should prompt urgent thyroid function testing
reference.pathophysiology: Amiodarone contains a large iodine load and is structurally similar to thyroid hormone, allowing it to disrupt thyroid function by several mechanisms. In type 1 disease, the iodine excess drives unregulated hormone synthesis in a gland with underlying autonomy, such as a multinodular goitre or subclinical Graves disease (the Jod-Basedow phenomenon). In type 2 disease, direct drug and iodine toxicity causes a destructive thyroiditis that releases stored thyroid hormone from an otherwise normal gland. Because these mechanisms differ fundamentally, they demand different treatments, and the two processes can coexist as a mixed form.
additionalDifferentials: Toxic multinodular goitre or toxic adenoma
Non-thyroidal illness with abnormal thyroid tests
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests (TSH, free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine)
Colour-flow Doppler ultrasound to assess gland vascularity
Radioiodine uptake where feasible, typically low in type 2
Inflammatory markers and interleukin-6 as adjuncts in some settings
Cardiac assessment given the underlying indication for amiodarone
redFlags: Thyrotoxic exacerbation of the underlying arrhythmia or heart failure
Rapid clinical deterioration in an amiodarone-treated patient
Refractory thyrotoxicosis where the type cannot be determined and disease progresses
reference.prognosis: Type 2 disease often remits over weeks to months with glucocorticoids, whereas type 1 usually requires antithyroid drugs and sometimes definitive treatment; overall outcome is influenced by the underlying cardiac disease and whether amiodarone can be discontinued.
pitfalls: Treating all cases as one entity and choosing the wrong drug for the type
Assuming stopping amiodarone alone will resolve thyrotoxicosis, given its long half-life
Overlooking a mixed form that needs combined therapy
Failing to recognise thyrotoxicosis as the cause of worsening arrhythmia
Discontinuing amiodarone abruptly without cardiology input when it is essential for arrhythmia control
references: Thyroid society guidance on amiodarone and thyroid dysfunction
management: Distinguish type 1 from type 2 disease using colour-flow Doppler and clinical features, as this determines therapy
Treat type 1 iodine-induced excess synthesis with antithyroid drugs such as carbimazole, sometimes with potassium perchlorate to block further iodine uptake
Treat type 2 destructive thyroiditis with oral glucocorticoids such as prednisolone
Use combined antithyroid drug and glucocorticoid therapy for mixed or indeterminate cases
Control adrenergic symptoms with a beta-blocker where not contraindicated by the underlying cardiac disease
Decide jointly with cardiology whether amiodarone can be withdrawn, weighing the arrhythmia indication
Consider total thyroidectomy for refractory thyrotoxicosis or when rapid control is needed in unstable cardiac disease, and offer radioiodine to type 1 once uptake recovers
Monitor thyroid function throughout treatment and remain alert for recurrence months after the drug is stopped
